title: Ἀπὸ Νισύρου ἐς Μάγνητας
titleEn: From Nisyrus to the Magnetes — Iliad 2.676–779
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The Catalogue of Ships goes on with its last contingents. Pheidippus and Antiphus bring thirty ships from Nisyrus, Cos and the neighbouring places, and Achilles has fifty ships of Myrmidons from Phthia and Hellas, who do not fight because he lies among the ships, angry over Briseis. The rest come from Thessaly and the north-west. Protesilaus, killed as he leapt first of the Achaeans from his ship, has his troops marshalled by his younger brother Podarces; Eumelus, son of Admetus, brings eleven ships; Philoctetes lies in pain on Lemnos from a snake’s bite while Medon commands his seven ships; the sons of Asclepius, Eurypylus, Polypoetes with Leonteus, Gouneus and Prothous follow, each with his ships. The poet then asks the Muse who was the best of the men and horses, and answers: the mares of “Pheres’ son” (usually taken to be Admetus), which Eumelus drives, and, while Achilles is wrathful, Ajax. The Catalogue closes on an idle army: Achilles lies by the ships, the troops play at discus, javelin and bow on the shore, the horses graze beside their chariots, and the men wander about missing their commander.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἄρα Νίσυρόν τ’ εἶχον Κράπαθόν τε Κάσον τε
καὶ Κῶν Εὐρυπύλοιο πόλιν νήσους τε Καλύδνας,
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ ara Nisyron t’ eichon Krapathon te Kason te
kai Kōn Eurypyloio polin nēsous te Kalydnas,
sentences.l:
And those who held Nisyrus and Crapathus and Casus
and Cos, the city of Eurypylus, and the islands Calydnae,
sentences.i: And those who held Nisyrus, Crapathus and Casus, and Cos, the city of Eurypylus, and the Calydnian islands,
sentences.n: The Catalogue goes on from Syme, at the end of the last part, to the places named here, in a new paragraph. οἳ δ’ ἄρα … εἶχον is ‘and those who held’, and εἶχον governs all the names that follow. Κῶν is the accusative of the name Cos, and Εὐρυπύλοιο is the epic genitive of Εὐρύπυλος, ‘of Eurypylus’, with πόλιν ‘city’ in apposition to Κῶν. Καλύδνας is the accusative plural of the group’s name, and νήσους τε ‘and the islands’ stands before it.

sentences.t:
τῶν αὖ Φείδιππός τε καὶ Ἄντιφος ἡγησάσθην
Θεσσαλοῦ υἷε δύω Ἡρακλεΐδαο ἄνακτος·
sentences.tr:
tōn au Pheidippos te kai Antiphos hēgēsasthēn
Thessalou huie dyō Hērakleïdao anaktos·
sentences.l:
Of these, in turn, Pheidippus and Antiphus led,
the two sons of Thessalus, Heracles’-son, the lord;
sentences.i: Of these, in turn, Pheidippus and Antiphus led, the two sons of lord Thessalus, the son of Heracles;
sentences.n: τῶν αὖ ‘of these, in turn’ opens the usual leader formula, but the verb is ἡγησάσθην, a dual aorist of ἡγέομαι ‘lead’, because two men lead together; υἷε δύω ‘two sons’ is dual too. Θεσσαλοῦ is the genitive of Θεσσαλός, the father, and Ἡρακλεΐδαο is a patronymic in the epic genitive -αο, ‘son of Heracles’, agreeing with Θεσσαλοῦ, with ἄνακτος ‘lord’ after it.

sentences.t: τοῖς δὲ τριήκοντα γλαφυραὶ νέες ἐστιχόωντο.
sentences.tr: tois de triēkonta glaphyrai nees estichoōnto.
sentences.l: and for them thirty hollow ships went in line.
sentences.i: and thirty hollow ships went in line with them.
sentences.n: The ships of this entry; the line is the same as 516. τοῖς is ‘for them’, the two leaders, and τριήκοντα ‘thirty’ is the number. γλαφυραί ‘hollow’ is the stock epithet of ships. ἐστιχόωντο is the imperfect of στιχάομαι ‘go in line’, with the epic stretched -όω-.

sentences.t:
νῦν αὖ τοὺς ὅσσοι τὸ Πελασγικὸν Ἄργος ἔναιον,
οἵ τ’ Ἄλον οἵ τ’ Ἀλόπην οἵ τε Τρηχῖνα νέμοντο,
sentences.tr:
nyn au tous hossoi to Pelasgikon Argos enaion,
hoi t’ Alon hoi t’ Alopēn hoi te Trēchina nemonto,
sentences.l:
Now, in turn, those, as many as the Pelasgian Argos dwelt in,
both who Alus and who Alope and who Trachis inhabited,
sentences.i: Now, in turn, as for all those who dwelt in Pelasgian Argos, and who inhabited Alus, Alope and Trachis,
sentences.n: A new entry, and its first words are an accusative that hangs until 685: νῦν αὖ τοὺς ὅσσοι … ἔναιον is ‘now, in turn, those, as many as dwelt in…’, and τῶν αὖ at 685 takes it up with ‘of these’. ἔναιον is the imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell in’. Πελασγικὸν Ἄργος is ‘Pelasgian Argos’, a district of northern Greece, not the Argos of the Peloponnese met in the entries before. οἵ τ’ … οἵ τ’ … οἵ τε is ‘both those who … and those who … and those who’, with νέμοντο ‘inhabited’ (νέμομαι) and the accusatives Ἄλον, Ἀλόπην and Τρηχῖνα.

sentences.t:
οἵ τ’ εἶχον Φθίην ἠδ’ Ἑλλάδα καλλιγύναικα,
Μυρμιδόνες δὲ καλεῦντο καὶ Ἕλληνες καὶ Ἀχαιοί,
sentences.tr:
hoi t’ eichon Phthiēn ēd’ Hellada kalligynaika,
Myrmidones de kaleunto kai Hellēnes kai Achaioi,
sentences.l:
and who held Phthia and Hellas of the fair women,
and were called Myrmidons and Hellenes and Achaeans,
sentences.i: and who held Phthia and Hellas of the fair women, and were called Myrmidons, Hellenes and Achaeans,
sentences.n: οἵ τ’ εἶχον is ‘and who held’, with Φθίην ‘Phthia’ and Ἑλλάδα καλλιγύναικα ‘Hellas of the fair women’, καλλιγύναικα being ‘with beautiful women’ (the Odyssey has it of Sparta). Here Ἑλλάς is a district beside Phthia, not the whole of Greece, and Ἕλληνες ‘Hellenes’ are its people. καλεῦντο is the epic imperfect passive of καλέω ‘call’ (Attic ἐκαλοῦντο), so the three names are all of this one people: Μυρμιδόνες, Ἕλληνες and Ἀχαιοί. Ἀχαιοί, here a local name, is also the poem’s name for the whole army.

sentences.t: τῶν αὖ πεντήκοντα νεῶν ἦν ἀρχὸς Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.tr: tōn au pentēkonta neōn ēn archos Achilleus.
sentences.l: Of these, in turn, of fifty ships was commander Achilles.
sentences.i: Of these, in turn, Achilles was commander of fifty ships.
sentences.n: τῶν αὖ ‘of these, in turn’ takes up the accusative that opened the entry at 681. ἦν ἀρχός is ‘was commander’, and ἀρχός takes the genitive πεντήκοντα νεῶν ‘of fifty ships’, which gives the size of the force. Achilles is named last in the sentence, and the next lines say why he does not lead his men.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οἵ γ’ οὐ πολέμοιο δυσηχέος ἐμνώοντο·
sentences.tr: all’ hoi g’ ou polemoio dysēcheos emnōonto·
sentences.l: But they were not mindful of ill-sounding war;
sentences.i: But they gave no thought to ill-sounding war;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οἵ γ’ ‘but they’ turns from the numbers to the men’s idleness. ἐμνώοντο is the epic imperfect of μνάομαι ‘be mindful of, think of’, with the genitive πολέμοιο ‘of war’. δυσηχής ‘ill-sounding’ is built on δυσ- ‘ill’ and ἦχος ‘sound’, an epithet of war for its din.

sentences.t: οὐ γὰρ ἔην ὅς τίς σφιν ἐπὶ στίχας ἡγήσαιτο·
sentences.tr: ou gar eēn hos tis sphin epi stichas hēgēsaito·
sentences.l: for there was not anyone who might lead them to the ranks;
sentences.i: for there was no one to lead them to the ranks;
sentences.n: The reason: οὐ γὰρ ἔην ‘for there was not’, ἔην being the epic imperfect of εἰμί. ὅς τίς is the relative with an indefinite sense, ‘anyone who’, and ἡγήσαιτο is the aorist optative middle of ἡγέομαι ‘lead’; the optative says what kind of man was lacking. σφιν is the dative ‘them’, and ἐπὶ στίχας ‘to the ranks’ (στίχες are the rows of fighting men).

sentences.t:
κεῖτο γὰρ ἐν νήεσσι ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεὺς
κούρης χωόμενος Βρισηΐδος ἠϋκόμοιο,
sentences.tr:
keito gar en nēessi podarkēs dios Achilleus
kourēs chōomenos Brisēïdos ēÿkomoio,
sentences.l:
for there lay among the ships swift-footed, heavenly Achilles,
incensed over the girl Briseis, fine-haired,
sentences.i: for swift-footed, heavenly Achilles lay among the ships, incensed over the fine-haired girl Briseis,
sentences.n: The man who should lead them: κεῖτο ‘lay’ is the imperfect of κεῖμαι, and ἐν νήεσσι is ‘among the ships’, with the epic dative plural -εσσι. Achilles has his stock epithets, ποδάρκης ‘swift-footed’ (the formation is uncertain, probably πούς + ἀρκέω) and δῖος ‘heavenly’. χωόμενος ‘incensed’ takes the genitive κούρης ‘over the girl’, and Βρισηΐδος ἠϋκόμοιο is ‘Briseis, fine-haired’, ἠΰκομος being the epithet the poem also gives to Leto.

sentences.t:
τὴν ἐκ Λυρνησσοῦ ἐξείλετο πολλὰ μογήσας
Λυρνησσὸν διαπορθήσας καὶ τείχεα Θήβης,
sentences.tr:
tēn ek Lyrnēssou exeileto polla mogēsas
Lyrnēsson diaporthēsas kai teichea Thēbēs,
sentences.l:
whom out of Lyrnessus he took for himself, having toiled much,
having sacked Lyrnessus and the walls of Thebe,
sentences.i: whom he took for himself out of Lyrnessus after much toil, having sacked Lyrnessus and the walls of Thebe,
sentences.n: τὴν is the relative ‘whom’, Briseis, and ἐκ Λυρνησσοῦ is ‘out of Lyrnessus’. ἐξείλετο is the aorist middle of ἐξαιρέω ‘take out’, and the middle makes it ‘took for himself’. πολλὰ μογήσας is ‘having toiled much’, the aorist participle of μογέω ‘toil’ with πολλά as an adverb. διαπορθήσας is the aorist participle of διαπορθέω, formed on πορθέω (a by-form of πέρθω ‘sack’) with δια- ‘through’; its objects are Λυρνησσόν and τείχεα Θήβης ‘the walls of Thebe’, a town name in the singular.

sentences.t:
κὰδ δὲ Μύνητ’ ἔβαλεν καὶ Ἐπίστροφον ἐγχεσιμώρους,
υἱέας Εὐηνοῖο Σεληπιάδαο ἄνακτος·
sentences.tr:
kad de Mynēt’ ebalen kai Epistrophon enchesimōrous,
huieas Euēnoio Selēpiadao anaktos·
sentences.l:
and he struck down Mynes and Epistrophus, spear-wielding,
sons of Euenus, Selepus’-son, the lord;
sentences.i: and he struck down Mynes and Epistrophus, spear-wielding sons of lord Euenus, the son of Selepus;
sentences.n: κὰδ δέ is κατὰ δέ, and with ἔβαλεν it is one verb split by tmesis: κατέβαλεν ‘struck down’, the aorist of καταβάλλω. Μύνης and Ἐπίστροφος are the two men struck down; this Epistrophus is not the Phocian leader of 517, for his father is named here as Euenus. ἐγχεσιμώρους is ‘spear-wielding’, an accusative adjective with the names, and the Odyssey uses it of the Myrmidons. Σεληπιάδαο is a patronymic in the epic genitive -αο, ‘son of Selepus’, and ἄνακτος ‘lord’ stands last, in the same case as Εὐηνοῖο and Σεληπιάδαο.

sentences.t: τῆς ὅ γε κεῖτ’ ἀχέων, τάχα δ’ ἀνστήσεσθαι ἔμελλεν.
sentences.tr: tēs ho ge keit’ acheōn, tacha d’ anstēsesthai emellen.
sentences.l: For her he lay grieving, and soon he was going to rise up.
sentences.i: He lay grieving for her, but soon he was to rise up.
sentences.n: τῆς ὅ γε is ‘for her, he’: τῆς is the genitive of cause, Briseis, and ὅ γε is Achilles, with stress. κεῖτ’ is κεῖτο ‘lay’, elided, and ἀχέων is the participle of ἀχέω ‘grieve’. ἀνστήσεσθαι is the future infinitive middle of ἀνίστημι ‘rise up’, in the epic form with ἀνα- shortened to ἀν-, and ἔμελλεν with an infinitive says what was bound to happen. The poet looks ahead to the end of the withdrawal.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ εἶχον Φυλάκην καὶ Πύρασον ἀνθεμόεντα
Δήμητρος τέμενος, Ἴτωνά τε μητέρα μήλων,
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ eichon Phylakēn kai Pyrason anthemoenta
Dēmētros temenos, Itōna te mētera mēlōn,
sentences.l:
And those who held Phylace and flowery Pyrasus,
the precinct of Demeter, and Iton, mother of flocks,
sentences.i: And those who held Phylace and flowery Pyrasus, the precinct of Demeter, and Iton, mother of flocks,
sentences.n: A new people, in a new paragraph: οἳ δ’ εἶχον is ‘and those who held’, with Φυλάκην ‘Phylace’ and Πύρασον ἀνθεμόεντα ‘flowery Pyrasus’, ἀνθεμόεις being ‘flowery’ (from ἄνθεμον ‘flower’). Δήμητρος τέμενος is ‘the precinct of Demeter’, in apposition to Pyrasus: a τέμενος is a piece of land set apart for a god. Ἴτωνά τε μητέρα μήλων is ‘and Iton, mother of flocks’, μῆλα being sheep and goats, so that ‘mother’ says Iton breeds them.

sentences.t: ἀγχίαλόν τ’ Ἀντρῶνα ἰδὲ Πτελεὸν λεχεποίην,
sentences.tr: anchialon t’ Antrōna ide Pteleon lechepoiēn,
sentences.l: and Antron near the sea, and Pteleum, grass-bedded,
sentences.i: and Antron near the sea, and Pteleum with its beds of grass,
sentences.n: The list goes on in the accusative. ἀγχίαλον ‘near the sea’ is ἀγχί ‘near’ + ἅλς ‘sea’, as of Chalcis at 640, and ἰδέ is the epic ‘and’ (= ἠδέ). Πτελεόν is Pteleum, and λεχεποίην is ‘grass-bedded’, from λέχος ‘bed’ and ποίη ‘grass’; the word is rare, and ‘with beds of grass’ is the usual explanation.

sentences.t:
τῶν αὖ Πρωτεσίλαος ἀρήϊος ἡγεμόνευε
ζωὸς ἐών·
sentences.tr:
tōn au Prōtesilaos arēïos hēgemoneue
zōos eōn·
sentences.l:
Of these, in turn, warlike Protesilaus was leader,
while he was alive;
sentences.i: Of these, in turn, warlike Protesilaus was the leader, while he lived;
sentences.n: τῶν αὖ … ἡγεμόνευε is the leader formula, ‘of these, in turn, was leader’ (αὖ here in place of the αὖθ’ of 540, 552, 563 and 601). Πρωτεσίλαος has the epithet ἀρήϊος ‘warlike’. ζωὸς ἐών is ‘while he was alive’, with ζωός the Ionic adjective ‘alive’ (Attic ζῶν) and ἐών the epic participle of εἰμί; the unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 699, and the next words say that he is already dead.

sentences.t: τότε δ’ ἤδη ἔχεν κάτα γαῖα μέλαινα.
sentences.tr: tote d’ ēdē echen kata gaia melaina.
sentences.l: but then already the dark earth held him down.
sentences.i: but by then the dark earth already held him.
sentences.n: τότε ‘at that time’ is the time of the muster, and ἤδη ‘already’ stresses how soon he was dead. ἔχεν κάτα is one verb, κατεῖχεν ‘held down’, with the preposition set after it (tmesis) and ἔχεν the unaugmented imperfect of ἔχω. γαῖα μέλαινα ‘the dark earth’ is a standing phrase, with μέλαινα ‘dark’ here and ‘black’ of the ships at 710.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δὲ καὶ ἀμφιδρυφὴς ἄλοχος Φυλάκῃ ἐλέλειπτο
καὶ δόμος ἡμιτελής·
sentences.tr:
tou de kai amphidryphēs alochos Phylakēi eleleipto
kai domos hēmitelēs·
sentences.l:
And of him also his wife, torn on both sides, in Phylace had been left,
and his house half-finished;
sentences.i: His wife, too, had been left behind in Phylace with her cheeks torn in mourning, and his house half-finished;
sentences.n: What he left at home. τοῦ δὲ καί is ‘and of him also’ (the genitive says whose wife and whose house). ἀμφιδρυφής ‘torn on both sides’ is built on ἀμφί ‘on both sides’ and δρύπτω ‘tear’, and the usual explanation is that the wife has torn her cheeks in mourning; the Greek says only ‘torn all round’. ἄλοχος is ‘wife’, Φυλάκῃ is the dative of place, ‘in Phylace’, and ἐλέλειπτο is the pluperfect passive of λείπω ‘leave’. δόμος ἡμιτελής is ‘a house half-finished’, begun and not completed. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 701.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἔκτανε Δάρδανος ἀνὴρ
νηὸς ἀποθρῴσκοντα πολὺ πρώτιστον Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
ton d’ ektane Dardanos anēr
nēos apothrōiskonta poly prōtiston Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
and him a Dardanian man killed,
as he leapt from the ship, by far the first of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: and a Dardanian man killed him as he leapt from his ship, by far the first of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ is ‘and him’, Protesilaus, with the article as a pronoun, and ἔκτανε is the epic aorist of κτείνω ‘kill’. Δάρδανος ἀνήρ is ‘a Dardanian man’, a Trojan-side warrior who is not named. νηὸς ἀποθρῴσκοντα is ‘as he leapt from the ship’ (νηός is the epic genitive of ναῦς, and ἀποθρῴσκοντα an accusative participle of ἀποθρῴσκω). πολὺ πρώτιστον Ἀχαιῶν is ‘by far the first of the Achaeans’; the Greek does not say first to do what, but the leap from the ship shows that it is to land.

sentences.t: οὐδὲ μὲν οὐδ’ οἳ ἄναρχοι ἔσαν, πόθεόν γε μὲν ἀρχόν·
sentences.tr: oude men oud’ hoi anarchoi esan, potheon ge men archon·
sentences.l: Nor indeed were even these without a commander, though they longed for their commander;
sentences.i: Yet they were not without a commander, though they missed their commander;
sentences.n: οὐδὲ μὲν οὐδ’ is a strong double negative, ‘nor indeed even’, and οἳ ‘those’ are the men of Protesilaus. ἄναρχοι ‘without a commander’ is ἀ- + ἀρχός ‘commander’, and ἔσαν is the epic ἦσαν. πόθεον is the imperfect of ποθέω ‘long for’, and γε μέν gives the contrast, ‘though they did’. The poet repeats the word, ἄναρχοι … ἀρχόν. The same line comes again at 726, for the men of Philoctetes.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά σφεας κόσμησε Ποδάρκης ὄζος Ἄρηος
Ἰφίκλου υἱὸς πολυμήλου Φυλακίδαο
αὐτοκασίγνητος μεγαθύμου Πρωτεσιλάου
ὁπλότερος γενεῇ·
sentences.tr:
alla spheas kosmēse Podarkēs ozos Arēos
Iphiklou huios polymēlou Phylakidao
autokasignētos megathymou Prōtesilaou
hoploteros geneēi·
sentences.l:
but them Podarces set in order, scion of Ares,
son of Iphiclus, rich in flocks, Phylacus’-son,
own brother of great-hearted Protesilaus,
the younger by birth;
sentences.i: but Podarces, scion of Ares, marshalled them: the son of Iphiclus, rich in flocks, who was the son of Phylacus, own brother of great-hearted Protesilaus, and younger by birth;
sentences.n: The man who took his place. σφεας is the epic accusative ‘them’, and κόσμησε is the aorist of κοσμέω ‘set in order’, here ‘marshal’. Ποδάρκης is a man’s name, the same word as the epithet ποδάρκης ‘swift-footed’ of Achilles at 688. ὄζος Ἄρηος is ‘scion of Ares’ (ὄζος is literally ‘branch’). His descent follows: Ἰφίκλου υἱός ‘son of Iphiclus’, πολυμήλου ‘rich in flocks’ (πολύ + μῆλα), and Φυλακίδαο, an epic patronymic genitive agreeing with Ἰφίκλου, ‘son of Phylacus’. αὐτοκασίγνητος is ‘own brother’, with the genitive Πρωτεσιλάου, and ὁπλότερος γενεῇ is ‘younger by birth’, with the dative of respect. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 707.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἅμα πρότερος καὶ ἀρείων
ἥρως Πρωτεσίλαος ἀρήϊος·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ hama proteros kai areiōn
hērōs Prōtesilaos arēïos·
sentences.l:
and he at once the elder and the braver,
the hero Protesilaus, warlike;
sentences.i: and the hero Protesilaus, the warlike, was at once the elder and the braver;
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ ‘and he’ is Protesilaus, who is named in the next line, and the Greek has no verb, so the English supplies ‘was’. ἅμα … καί is ‘at once … and’. πρότερος is ‘elder’, the comparative of πρό in the sense ‘born before’, and ἀρείων is a comparative ‘better’ from the family of ἀρετή, taken here as ‘braver’. ἀρήϊος ‘warlike’ repeats the epithet of 698. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 708.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι λαοὶ
δεύονθ’ ἡγεμόνος, πόθεόν γε μὲν ἐσθλὸν ἐόντα·
sentences.tr:
oude ti laoi
deuonth’ hēgemonos, potheon ge men esthlon eonta·
sentences.l:
nor did the people at all
lack a leader, though they longed for him, being good;
sentences.i: nor did the troops lack a leader at all, though they missed him, good man that he was;
sentences.n: οὐδέ τι is ‘nor at all’, and δεύονθ’ is the imperfect δεύοντο of δεύομαι ‘lack’, elided before the rough breathing of ἡγεμόνος, with the genitive ἡγεμόνος ‘of a leader’; the subject is λαοί ‘people’, here the troops of one contingent. πόθεον … γε μέν repeats the verb of 703, ‘though they longed for’, and ἐσθλὸν ἐόντα ‘being good’ is an accusative participle agreeing with the man they miss, Protesilaus: they have a leader in Podarces, but it is the good one they have lost that they long for.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἅμα τεσσαράκοντα μέλαιναι νῆες ἕποντο.
sentences.tr: tōi d’ hama tessarakonta melainai nēes heponto.
sentences.l: And with him forty black ships followed.
sentences.i: And with him forty black ships followed.
sentences.n: The formula that closes an entry, as at 524 and 534: τῷ δ’ ἅμα … ‘and with him’, singular because one man leads, then τεσσαράκοντα ‘forty’, μέλαιναι νῆες ‘black ships’ and ἕποντο, the unaugmented imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’. Here the sentence ends with the line.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ Φερὰς ἐνέμοντο παραὶ Βοιβηΐδα λίμνην
Βοίβην καὶ Γλαφύρας καὶ ἐϋκτιμένην Ἰαωλκόν,
sentences.tr:
hoi de Pheras enemonto parai Boibēïda limnēn
Boibēn kai Glaphyras kai eÿktimenēn Iaōlkon,
sentences.l:
And those who inhabited Pherae beside the Boebeian lake,
Boebe and Glaphyrae and well-built Iolcus,
sentences.i: And those who inhabited Pherae beside the Boebeian lake, Boebe, Glaphyrae and well-built Iolcus,
sentences.n: A new entry: οἳ δὲ Φερὰς ἐνέμοντο is ‘and those who inhabited Pherae’, Φεράς being the accusative plural of the name. παραί is the epic παρά ‘beside’, and Βοιβηΐδα λίμνην is ‘the Boebeian lake’, Βοιβηΐς being the adjective of Βοίβη, the town named next. Βοίβην, Γλαφύρας and Ἰαωλκόν are three more accusatives, and ἐϋκτιμένην ‘well-built’ is the stock epithet of a settlement, as of Cleonae at 570.

sentences.t:
τῶν ἦρχ’ Ἀδμήτοιο φίλος πάϊς ἕνδεκα νηῶν
Εὔμηλος, τὸν ὑπ’ Ἀδμήτῳ τέκε δῖα γυναικῶν
Ἄλκηστις Πελίαο θυγατρῶν εἶδος ἀρίστη.
sentences.tr:
tōn ērch’ Admētoio philos païs hendeka nēōn
Eumēlos, ton hyp’ Admētōi teke dia gynaikōn
Alkēstis Peliao thygatrōn eidos aristē.
sentences.l:
Of these was leading, of eleven ships, Admetus’ dear son
Eumelus, whom to Admetus bore, heavenly-one of women,
Alcestis, of Pelias’ daughters in form the best.
sentences.i: Of these, Admetus’ dear son Eumelus led eleven ships, whom Alcestis bore to Admetus, heavenly among women, the best in looks of the daughters of Pelias.
sentences.n: τῶν ἦρχ’ is ‘of these was leading’, ἄρχω taking the genitive of the people and ἕνδεκα νηῶν ‘of eleven ships’ giving the size; the leader’s name Εὔμηλος is held back to the next line, after Ἀδμήτοιο φίλος πάϊς ‘Admetus’ dear son’. τὸν ὑπ’ Ἀδμήτῳ τέκε is ‘whom she bore to Admetus’, ὑπό with the dative being the idiom for bearing a child to a man. δῖα γυναικῶν ‘heavenly among women’ is the Odyssey’s phrase for Penelope and for Helen, and the mother’s name, Ἄλκηστις, is held back until after her epithet; Πελίαο θυγατρῶν εἶδος ἀρίστη is ‘the best of the daughters of Pelias in looks’, with εἶδος an accusative of respect, as the Odyssey says of Periboea.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἄρα Μηθώνην καὶ Θαυμακίην ἐνέμοντο
καὶ Μελίβοιαν ἔχον καὶ Ὀλιζῶνα τρηχεῖαν,
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ ara Mēthōnēn kai Thaumakiēn enemonto
kai Meliboian echon kai Olizōna trēcheian,
sentences.l:
And those who inhabited Methone and Thaumacia
and held Meliboea and rough Olizon,
sentences.i: And those who inhabited Methone and Thaumacia, and held Meliboea and rough Olizon,
sentences.n: A new entry: οἳ δ’ ἄρα … ἐνέμοντο is ‘and those who inhabited’, with Μηθώνην and Θαυμακίην, and the list goes on with ἔχον ‘held’ for Μελίβοιαν and Ὀλιζῶνα. τρηχεῖαν is ‘rough’, the feminine of τρηχύς, the word the poem also uses of Aegilips and the Odyssey of Ithaca.

sentences.t:
τῶν δὲ Φιλοκτήτης ἦρχεν τόξων ἐῢ εἰδὼς
ἑπτὰ νεῶν·
sentences.tr:
tōn de Philoktētēs ērchen toxōn eÿ eidōs
hepta neōn·
sentences.l:
Of these Philoctetes was leading, well knowing the bow,
of seven ships;
sentences.i: Of these Philoctetes, who knew the bow well, led seven ships;
sentences.n: τῶν δέ is ‘of these’, and Φιλοκτήτης ἦρχεν ‘Philoctetes was leading’ takes ἑπτὰ νεῶν ‘of seven ships’ in the next half-line. τόξων ἐῢ εἰδώς is ‘knowing the bow well’: εἰδώς, the perfect participle of οἶδα, takes the genitive τόξων, and τόξα is the plural used for a single bow. The same phrase comes back in the next line. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 719.

sentences.t:
ἐρέται δ’ ἐν ἑκάστῃ πεντήκοντα
ἐμβέβασαν τόξων εὖ εἰδότες ἶφι μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
eretai d’ en hekastēi pentēkonta
embebasan toxōn eu eidotes iphi machesthai.
sentences.l:
and oarsmen in each, fifty,
had embarked, well knowing the bow, with force to fight.
sentences.i: and in each ship fifty oarsmen were on board, men who knew the bow well, for fighting powerfully.
sentences.n: ἐρέται ‘oarsmen’ and ἐν ἑκάστῃ ‘in each’ (ship) with πεντήκοντα ‘fifty’ say that every ship has fifty rowers, who are also archers. ἐμβέβασαν is the epic pluperfect of ἐμβαίνω ‘go aboard’ (formed like ἕστασαν at 777): ‘had gone aboard’, that is ‘were on board’. τόξων εὖ εἰδότες repeats the phrase of 718 in the plural, and ἶφι μάχεσθαι is ‘to fight powerfully’ (ἶφι ‘with force’), the infinitive saying what they were there for.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὃ μὲν ἐν νήσῳ κεῖτο κρατέρ’ ἄλγεα πάσχων
Λήμνῳ ἐν ἠγαθέῃ, ὅθι μιν λίπον υἷες Ἀχαιῶν
ἕλκεϊ μοχθίζοντα κακῷ ὀλοόφρονος ὕδρου·
sentences.tr:
all’ ho men en nēsōi keito krater’ algea paschōn
Lēmnōi en ēgatheēi, hothi min lipon huies Achaiōn
helkeï mochthizonta kakōi oloophronos hydrou·
sentences.i: But he lay on an island suffering harsh pains, in holy Lemnos, where the sons of the Achaeans had left him, suffering from the evil wound of a baleful-minded water-snake;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὃ μὲν is ‘but he’, Philoctetes, and ἐν νήσῳ κεῖτο κρατέρ’ ἄλγεα πάσχων is ‘lay on an island suffering harsh pains’, the same half-lines the Odyssey has of Odysseus on Calypso’s island. The island is named in the next line, Λήμνῳ ἐν ἠγαθέῃ ‘in holy Lemnos’, and ὅθι μιν λίπον is ‘where they left him’. υἷες Ἀχαιῶν is ‘the sons of the Achaeans’. ἕλκεϊ … κακῷ ‘by an evil wound’ is a dative of cause with μοχθίζοντα ‘toiling, suffering’ (μοχθίζω), and ὀλοόφρονος ὕδρου is ‘of a baleful-minded water-snake’: ὕδρος is a snake of the water, and ὀλοόφρων ‘baleful-minded’ is the epithet the Odyssey gives to Atlas, Aeetes and Minos.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ ὅ γε κεῖτ’ ἀχέων·
sentences.tr: enth’ ho ge keit’ acheōn·
sentences.l: There he lay grieving;
sentences.i: There he lay grieving;
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ ὅ γε κεῖτ’ ἀχέων is ‘there he lay grieving’, the same words as the Odyssey has of old Laertes and the same phrase as in 694, with ἔνθ’ ‘there’ for τῆς ‘for her’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 724.

sentences.t:
τάχα δὲ μνήσεσθαι ἔμελλον
Ἀργεῖοι παρὰ νηυσὶ Φιλοκτήταο ἄνακτος.
sentences.tr:
tacha de mnēsesthai emellon
Argeioi para nēusi Philoktētao anaktos.
sentences.l:
and soon were going to call to mind
the Argives, beside the ships, lord Philoctetes.
sentences.i: and soon the Argives beside the ships were to remember lord Philoctetes.
sentences.n: τάχα δὲ … ἔμελλον is ‘and soon they were going to’, with ἔμελλον and an infinitive as in 694. μνήσεσθαι is the future infinitive of μιμνήσκομαι ‘call to mind’, which takes the genitive Φιλοκτήταο ἄνακτος ‘lord Philoctetes’ (epic genitive -αο), and Ἀργεῖοι ‘Argives’ is the whole army, ‘beside the ships’.

sentences.t: οὐδὲ μὲν οὐδ’ οἳ ἄναρχοι ἔσαν, πόθεόν γε μὲν ἀρχόν·
sentences.tr: oude men oud’ hoi anarchoi esan, potheon ge men archon·
sentences.l: Nor indeed were even these without a commander, though they longed for their commander;
sentences.i: Yet they were not without a commander, though they missed their commander;
sentences.n: The line of 703, said now of the men of Philoctetes; for the words see the note there. The commander they miss is Philoctetes, left on Lemnos, and the next line names the man who set them in order.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ Μέδων κόσμησεν Ὀϊλῆος νόθος υἱός,
τόν ῥ’ ἔτεκεν Ῥήνη ὑπ’ Ὀϊλῆϊ πτολιπόρθῳ.
sentences.tr:
alla Medōn kosmēsen Oïlēos nothos huios,
ton rh’ eteken Rhēnē hyp’ Oïlēï ptoliporthōi.
sentences.l:
but Medon set them in order, Oileus’ bastard son,
whom bore Rhene to Oileus, the city-sacking.
sentences.i: but Medon marshalled them, the illegitimate son of Oileus, whom Rhene bore to Oileus, sacker of cities.
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ Μέδων κόσμησεν is ‘but Medon set in order’, with ‘them’ understood from the entry (compare 704). Ὀϊλῆος νόθος υἱός is ‘Oileus’ bastard son’, νόθος meaning born outside marriage; Oileus is also the father of swift Ajax at 527. τόν ῥ’ ἔτεκεν Ῥήνη ὑπ’ Ὀϊλῆϊ is ‘whom Rhene bore to Oileus’ (compare 714), and πτολιπόρθῳ ‘city-sacking’ is built on πτόλις (the epic πόλις) and πέρθω ‘sack’; the Odyssey has the longer πτολιπόρθιος for Odysseus.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ εἶχον Τρίκκην καὶ Ἰθώμην κλωμακόεσσαν,
οἵ τ’ ἔχον Οἰχαλίην πόλιν Εὐρύτου Οἰχαλιῆος,
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ eichon Trikkēn kai Ithōmēn klōmakoessan,
hoi t’ echon Oichaliēn polin Eurytou Oichaliēos,
sentences.l:
And those who held Tricca and stony Ithome,
and who held Oechalia, city of Eurytus the Oechalian,
sentences.i: And those who held Tricca and stony Ithome, and those who held Oechalia, the city of Eurytus the Oechalian,
sentences.n: A new entry: οἳ δ’ εἶχον ‘and those who held’ Τρίκκην and Ἰθώμην κλωμακόεσσαν. κλωμακόεις is built on κλῶμαξ, which is a heap of stones, so ‘stony’; whether it means stony or terraced is not certain. οἵ τ’ ἔχον adds Οἰχαλίην πόλιν Εὐρύτου Οἰχαλιῆος ‘Oechalia, the city of Eurytus the Oechalian’, Οἰχαλιῆος being the epic genitive of Οἰχαλιεύς, the Eurytus of 596.

sentences.t:
τῶν αὖθ’ ἡγείσθην Ἀσκληπιοῦ δύο παῖδε
ἰητῆρ’ ἀγαθὼ Ποδαλείριος ἠδὲ Μαχάων·
sentences.tr:
tōn auth’ hēgeisthēn Asklēpiou dyo paide
iētēr’ agathō Podaleirios ēde Machaōn·
sentences.l:
Of these, in turn, led the two sons of Asclepius,
two good healers, Podaleirius and Machaon;
sentences.i: Of these, in turn, the two sons of Asclepius led, good healers both, Podaleirius and Machaon;
sentences.n: τῶν αὖθ’ ἡγείσθην is ‘of these, in turn, led’, with ἡγείσθην the imperfect dual of ἡγέομαι, because two sons of Ἀσκληπιός lead together: Ἀσκληπιοῦ δύο παῖδε ‘the two sons of Asclepius’. ἰητῆρ’ ἀγαθὼ is ‘two good healers’, a dual in apposition (ἰητῆρ’ is the elided dual ἰητῆρε; ἰητήρ ‘healer’ is the Odyssey’s word), and the names follow. The unit ends at the ano teleia at the end of 732.

sentences.t: τοῖς δὲ τριήκοντα γλαφυραὶ νέες ἐστιχόωντο.
sentences.tr: tois de triēkonta glaphyrai nees estichoōnto.
sentences.l: and for them thirty hollow ships went in line.
sentences.i: and thirty hollow ships went in line with them.
sentences.n: The same closing line as 680: τοῖς is ‘for them’, the two sons of Asclepius, τριήκοντα ‘thirty’ is the number, and ἐστιχόωντο is the imperfect of στιχάομαι ‘go in line’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἔχον Ὀρμένιον, οἵ τε κρήνην Ὑπέρειαν,
οἵ τ’ ἔχον Ἀστέριον Τιτάνοιό τε λευκὰ κάρηνα,
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ echon Ormenion, hoi te krēnēn Hypereian,
hoi t’ echon Asterion Titanoio te leuka karēna,
sentences.l:
And those who held Ormenium, and who the spring Hypereia,
and who held Asterium and the white peaks of Titanus,
sentences.i: And those who held Ormenium, and those who held the spring Hypereia, and those who held Asterium and the white peaks of Titanus,
sentences.n: A new entry: οἳ δ’ ἔχον Ὀρμένιον is ‘and those who held Ormenium’, and οἵ τε κρήνην Ὑπέρειαν is ‘and those who (held) the spring Hypereia’, the verb being understood and Ὑπέρεια the spring’s name. οἵ τ’ ἔχον Ἀστέριον adds Asterium, and Τιτάνοιό τε λευκὰ κάρηνα is ‘and the white peaks of Titanus’: Τιτάνοιο is the epic genitive of Τίτανος, taken as a place-name (τίτανος is also the common word for ‘chalk, gypsum’, so the sense is not certain), and κάρηνα are literally ‘heads’, here the heights of a hill.

sentences.t: τῶν ἦρχ’ Εὐρύπυλος Εὐαίμονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός·
sentences.tr: tōn ērch’ Eurypylos Euaimonos aglaos huios·
sentences.l: Of these was leading Eurypylus, Euaemon’s splendid son;
sentences.i: Of these, Eurypylus, the splendid son of Euaemon, led;
sentences.n: τῶν ἦρχ’ is ‘of these was leading’, as at 713. Εὐρύπυλος Εὐαίμονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός is ‘Eurypylus, Euaemon’s splendid son’: Εὐαίμονος is the genitive of Εὐαίμων, and ἀγλαός ‘splendid’ is the Odyssey’s epithet for Nestor’s son. This Eurypylus is not the man of Cos at 677. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: the last syllable of Εὐρύπυλος is short but stands in a long place, at the main caesura before the vowel of Εὐαίμονος.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἅμα τεσσαράκοντα μέλαιναι νῆες ἕποντο.
sentences.tr: tōi d’ hama tessarakonta melainai nēes heponto.
sentences.l: And with him forty black ships followed.
sentences.i: And with him forty black ships followed.
sentences.n: The closing formula of 710 and 747, here with τῷ ‘with him’ for Eurypylus, the only leader of the entry. The line ends the sentence.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ Ἄργισσαν ἔχον καὶ Γυρτώνην ἐνέμοντο,
Ὄρθην Ἠλώνην τε πόλιν τ’ Ὀλοοσσόνα λευκήν,
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ Argissan echon kai Gyrtōnēn enemonto,
Orthēn Ēlōnēn te polin t’ Oloossona leukēn,
sentences.l:
And those who held Argissa and inhabited Gyrtone,
Orthe and Elone and the city Oloosson, the white,
sentences.i: And those who held Argissa and inhabited Gyrtone, Orthe and Elone, and the white city of Oloosson,
sentences.n: A new entry: οἳ δ’ Ἄργισσαν ἔχον is ‘and those who held Argissa’, and Γυρτώνην ἐνέμοντο ‘inhabited Gyrtone’. The list goes on in the accusative with Ὄρθην and Ἠλώνην, and πόλιν τ’ Ὀλοοσσόνα λευκήν is ‘and the city Oloosson, the white’, λευκός being the plain colour word, as in the white peaks of 735.

sentences.t:
τῶν αὖθ’ ἡγεμόνευε μενεπτόλεμος Πολυποίτης
υἱὸς Πειριθόοιο τὸν ἀθάνατος τέκετο Ζεύς·
sentences.tr:
tōn auth’ hēgemoneue meneptolemos Polypoitēs
huios Peirithooio ton athanatos teketo Zeus·
sentences.l:
Of these, in turn, was leader steadfast-in-battle Polypoetes,
son of Peirithous, whom immortal Zeus begot;
sentences.i: Of these, in turn, Polypoetes, steadfast in battle, was the leader, the son of Peirithous, whom immortal Zeus begot;
sentences.n: The leader formula τῶν αὖθ’ ἡγεμόνευε (698 has τῶν αὖ), with Πολυποίτης, whose epithet μενεπτόλεμος is ‘steadfast in battle’ (the Odyssey gives it to Thrasymedes). υἱὸς Πειριθόοιο is ‘son of Peirithous’, the epic genitive of Πειρίθοος, and τὸν ἀθάνατος τέκετο Ζεύς is ‘whom immortal Zeus begot’: τὸν is Peirithous, the object of τέκετο ‘begot’, the aorist of τίκτω said of a father. The unit ends at the ano teleia at the end of 741.

sentences.t:
τόν ῥ’ ὑπὸ Πειριθόῳ τέκετο κλυτὸς Ἱπποδάμεια
ἤματι τῷ ὅτε Φῆρας ἐτίσατο λαχνήεντας,
sentences.tr:
ton rh’ hypo Peirithoōi teketo klytos Hippodameia
ēmati tōi hote Phēras etisato lachnēentas,
sentences.l:
whom to Peirithous bore famous Hippodameia
on the day when he took vengeance on the hairy beasts,
sentences.i: whom famous Hippodameia bore to Peirithous on the day when he took vengeance on the hairy beasts,
sentences.n: τόν ῥ’ ὑπὸ Πειριθόῳ τέκετο … Ἱπποδάμεια is ‘whom Hippodameia bore to Peirithous’: τόν is now Polypoetes, ὑπό with the dative is the idiom of 714, and τέκετο is the verb of 741, now said of the mother. κλυτός ‘famous’ stands with the feminine name in a masculine form, as the edition prints it. ἤματι τῷ ὅτε is ‘on the day when’, and the subject of ἐτίσατο, Peirithous, is understood. Φῆρας ἐτίσατο is ‘took vengeance on the Φῆρες, the beasts’: ἐτίσατο is the aorist middle of τίνω, and φήρ is a wild beast (as in φηρσίν at 1.268); the Greek does not use the name Centaurs. λαχνήεντας is ‘hairy’.

sentences.t: τοὺς δ’ ἐκ Πηλίου ὦσε καὶ Αἰθίκεσσι πέλασσεν·
sentences.tr: tous d’ ek Pēliou ōse kai Aithikessi pelassen·
sentences.l: and them out of Pelion he thrust and to the Aethices brought them near;
sentences.i: and he pushed them out of Pelion and forced them on to the Aethices;
sentences.n: τοὺς δ’ is ‘and them’, the beasts. ὦσε is the aorist of ὠθέω ‘thrust, push’, ἐκ Πηλίου is ‘out of Pelion’ (the mountain of 757), and πέλασσεν is the aorist of πελάζω ‘bring near, drive to’, with the dative Αἰθίκεσσι, the epic dative plural of a people, the Aethices, of whom the Greek says no more. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οὐκ οἶος, ἅμα τῷ γε Λεοντεὺς ὄζος Ἄρηος
υἱὸς ὑπερθύμοιο Κορώνου Καινεΐδαο·
sentences.tr:
ouk oios, hama tōi ge Leonteus ozos Arēos
huios hyperthymoio Korōnou Kaineïdao·
sentences.l:
not alone, but with him Leonteus, scion of Ares,
son of high-spirited Coronus, Caeneus’-son;
sentences.i: He did not lead alone: with him was Leonteus, scion of Ares, son of high-spirited Coronus, the son of Caeneus;
sentences.n: The Greek has no verb: οὐκ οἶος ‘not alone’ and ἅμα τῷ γε ‘along with him’ say that Polypoetes did not lead alone (the English supplies ‘lead’ from 740), and Λεοντεύς is the second leader. ὄζος Ἄρηος ‘scion of Ares’ is the title given to Podarces at 704. ὑπερθύμοιο is ‘high-spirited’, the Odyssey’s epithet of Creon and of the Giants, and Κορώνου Καινεΐδαο is ‘Coronus, Caeneus’-son’, a patronymic with the epic genitive -αο.

sentences.t: τοῖς δ’ ἅμα τεσσαράκοντα μέλαιναι νῆες ἕποντο.
sentences.tr: tois d’ hama tessarakonta melainai nēes heponto.
sentences.l: And with them forty black ships followed.
sentences.i: And with them forty black ships followed.
sentences.n: The closing formula of 710 and 737, here with τοῖς ‘with them’ for the two leaders, Polypoetes and Leonteus, and the same line as 524.

sentences.t: Γουνεὺς δ’ ἐκ Κύφου ἦγε δύω καὶ εἴκοσι νῆας·
sentences.tr: Gouneus d’ ek Kyphou ēge dyō kai eikosi nēas·
sentences.l: And Gouneus from Cyphus brought two and twenty ships;
sentences.i: And Gouneus brought twenty-two ships from Cyphus;
sentences.n: A new entry: Γουνεὺς δ’ ἐκ Κύφου ἦγε is ‘and Gouneus from Cyphus brought’, with ἦγε the imperfect of ἄγω ‘bring’, kept apart from ἄρχω and ἡγεμονεύω ‘lead’. δύω καὶ εἴκοσι is ‘two and twenty’, and νῆας ‘ships’ comes last. The entry has no closing formula of its own; the next lines tell who followed him.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ Ἐνιῆνες ἕποντο μενεπτόλεμοί τε Περαιβοὶ
οἳ περὶ Δωδώνην δυσχείμερον οἰκί’ ἔθεντο,
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ Eniēnes heponto meneptolemoi te Peraiboi
hoi peri Dōdōnēn dyscheimeron oiki’ ethento,
sentences.l:
and with him followed the Enienes and the steadfast-in-battle Perrhaebi,
who around harsh-wintered Dodona made their homes,
sentences.i: and with him followed the Enienes and the Perrhaebi, steadfast in battle, who made their homes around Dodona of the harsh winters,
sentences.n: τῷ δ’ … ἕποντο is ‘and with him followed’, the verb of the closing formula, here said of peoples, not ships: Ἐνιῆνες ‘the Enienes’ and Περαιβοί ‘the Perrhaebi’, the second with the epithet μενεπτόλεμοι ‘steadfast in battle’ (see 740). οἳ περὶ Δωδώνην … οἰκί’ ἔθεντο is ‘who made their homes around Dodona’, οἰκί’ being οἰκία ‘homes’ and ἔθεντο the aorist middle of τίθημι. δυσχείμερον ‘harsh-wintered’ is δυσ- ‘ill’ + χεῖμα ‘winter’, agreeing with Δωδώνην.

sentences.t:
οἵ τ’ ἀμφ’ ἱμερτὸν Τιταρησσὸν ἔργα νέμοντο
ὅς ῥ’ ἐς Πηνειὸν προΐει καλλίρροον ὕδωρ,
sentences.tr:
hoi t’ amph’ himerton Titarēsson erga nemonto
hos rh’ es Pēneion proïei kallirroon hydōr,
sentences.l:
and who around lovely Titaressus inhabited the farmlands,
which into the Peneius sends its fair-flowing water,
sentences.i: and those who inhabited the farmlands around lovely Titaressus, a river that sends its fair-flowing water into the Peneius,
sentences.n: οἵ τ’ … ἔργα νέμοντο is ‘and who inhabited the fields’: ἔργα are the tilled lands, and νέμοντο is the imperfect of νέμομαι ‘inhabit’. ἱμερτὸν Τιταρησσόν is ‘lovely Titaressus’, ἱμερτός being ‘lovely’; the relative ὅς of the second line is masculine, so Titaressus is a river, and it ‘sends its water’ into another. προΐει is from προΐημι ‘send forth’, and καλλίρροον ὕδωρ is ‘fair-flowing water’, from καλλι- ‘fair’ and ῥόος ‘stream’. Πηνειόν is the river Peneius, named again in the next line and at 757.

sentences.t: οὐδ’ ὅ γε Πηνειῷ συμμίσγεται ἀργυροδίνῃ,
sentences.tr: oud’ ho ge Pēneiōi symmisgetai argyrodinēi,
sentences.l: and yet it does not mingle with Peneius, silver-eddying,
sentences.i: and yet it does not mingle with the silver-eddying Peneius,
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ὅ γε is ‘but it does not’: ὅ γε is the Titaressus, the subject of the sentence, and συμμίσγεται ‘mingles’ takes the dative Πηνειῷ. ἀργυροδίνῃ ‘silver-eddying’ is ἀργυρο- ‘silver’ + δίνη ‘eddy’, an epithet of rivers.

sentences.t: ἀλλά τέ μιν καθύπερθεν ἐπιρρέει ἠΰτ’ ἔλαιον·
sentences.tr: alla te min kathyperthen epirreei ēÿt’ elaion·
sentences.l: but over it, above, it flows, like olive-oil;
sentences.i: but flows over the top of it, like olive oil;
sentences.n: μιν is ‘it’, the Peneius, and τε in ἀλλά τέ marks a general fact. καθύπερθεν ‘above, on top’ goes with ἐπιρρέει ‘flows over’, and ἠΰτ’ ἔλαιον is ‘like olive oil’: ἠΰτε is ‘like’, and ἔλαιον is oil of the olive. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ὅρκου γὰρ δεινοῦ Στυγὸς ὕδατός ἐστιν ἀπορρώξ.
sentences.tr: horkou gar deinou Stygos hydatos estin aporrōx.
sentences.l: for of the dread oath, the water of the Styx, it is an offshoot.
sentences.i: for it is an offshoot of the water of the Styx, the dread oath.
sentences.n: The reason the two rivers do not mix. ὅρκου δεινοῦ Στυγὸς ὕδατος are three genitives in apposition, ‘of the dread oath, of the water of the Styx’ (the Styx’s water is what a dread oath was sworn by), and ἀπορρώξ is a piece broken off, ‘offshoot’, as the Odyssey says of Cocytus and the Styx’s water. The Greek means that the Titaressus is itself a branch of the Styx.

sentences.t: Μαγνήτων δ’ ἦρχε Πρόθοος Τενθρηδόνος υἱός,
sentences.tr: Magnētōn d’ ērche Prothoos Tenthrēdonos huios,
sentences.l: And of the Magnetes was leading Prothous, Tenthredon’s son,
sentences.i: And Prothous, the son of Tenthredon, led the Magnetes,
sentences.n: A new entry: Μαγνήτων δ’ ἦρχε is ‘and of the Magnetes was leading’, ἄρχω with the genitive of the people, as at 713 and 736. Πρόθοος Τενθρηδόνος υἱός is ‘Prothous, son of Tenthredon’, Τενθρηδόνος being the genitive of Τενθρηδών.

sentences.t:
οἳ περὶ Πηνειὸν καὶ Πήλιον εἰνοσίφυλλον
ναίεσκον·
sentences.tr:
hoi peri Pēneion kai Pēlion einosiphyllon
naieskon·
sentences.l:
who around the Peneius and leaf-shaking Pelion
kept dwelling;
sentences.i: who dwelt around the Peneius and leaf-shaking Pelion;
sentences.n: οἳ περὶ Πηνειὸν καὶ Πήλιον εἰνοσίφυλλον is ‘who around the Peneius and leaf-shaking Pelion’. εἰνοσίφυλλον ‘leaf-shaking’ is ἔνοσις ‘shaking’ + φύλλον ‘leaf’, an epithet the poem gives also to Neriton at 632. ναίεσκον is the iterative imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell’, and the suffix -σκ- gives ‘kept dwelling’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 758.

sentences.t: τῶν μὲν Πρόθοος θοὸς ἡγεμόνευε,
sentences.tr: tōn men Prothoos thoos hēgemoneue,
sentences.l: Of these Prothous, the swift, was leader,
sentences.i: Of these swift Prothous was the leader,
sentences.n: τῶν μέν is ‘of these’, and ἡγεμόνευε ‘was leader’ names Prothous a second time, now with the epithet θοός ‘swift’, a stock epithet that the poem uses of ships as well as men. ἦρχε in 756 and ἡγεμόνευε here are told apart in English as ‘led’ and ‘was the leader’.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἅμα τεσσαράκοντα μέλαιναι νῆες ἕποντο.
sentences.tr: tōi d’ hama tessarakonta melainai nēes heponto.
sentences.l: And with him forty black ships followed.
sentences.i: And with him forty black ships followed.
sentences.n: The closing formula of 710 and 737, here with τῷ ‘with him’ for Prothous. It ends the entry of the Magnetes, the last of the Catalogue of the Achaean ships.

sentences.t: οὗτοι ἄρ’ ἡγεμόνες Δαναῶν καὶ κοίρανοι ἦσαν·
sentences.tr: houtoi ar’ hēgemones Danaōn kai koiranoi ēsan·
sentences.l: These then were the leaders of the Danaans, and rulers;
sentences.i: These, then, were the leaders and rulers of the Danaans;
sentences.n: A new paragraph, which sums the Catalogue up. οὗτοι ἄρ’ is ‘these, then’, and ἡγεμόνες Δαναῶν καὶ κοίρανοι ἦσαν is ‘were leaders and rulers of the Danaans’, κοίρανος ‘ruler’ being the Odyssey’s word. Δαναῶν is one of the poem’s three names for the army.

sentences.t:
τίς τὰρ τῶν ὄχ’ ἄριστος ἔην σύ μοι ἔννεπε Μοῦσα
αὐτῶν ἠδ’ ἵππων, οἳ ἅμ’ Ἀτρεΐδῃσιν ἕποντο.
sentences.tr:
tis tar tōn och’ aristos eēn sy moi ennepe Mousa
autōn ēd’ hippōn, hoi ham’ Atreïdēisin heponto.
sentences.l:
Who then of these was by far the best — do you tell me, Muse —
of themselves and of the horses that together with the sons of Atreus followed.
sentences.i: Tell me, Muse, which of them was far the best, of the men themselves and of the horses that followed with the sons of Atreus.
sentences.n: The poet asks the Muse again (compare 484). τίς τὰρ τῶν is ‘who then of these’, τὰρ being τε ἄρα run together, as in τίς τ’ ἄρ at 1.8. The question is put inside a command, τίς … ἔννεπε ‘who … tell me’, and the edition ends it with a full stop, so the English does too. ὄχ’ ἄριστος ἔην is ‘was by far the best’ (ὄχα ‘by far’, as at 1.69), and σύ μοι ἔννεπε Μοῦσα ‘you, Muse, tell me’ breaks into it: ἔννεπε is the imperative of ἐννέπω ‘tell’. αὐτῶν ἠδ’ ἵππων is ‘of the men themselves and of the horses’, and οἳ ἅμ’ Ἀτρεΐδῃσιν ἕποντο ‘who followed with the sons of Atreus’ goes with both.

sentences.t: ἵπποι μὲν μέγ’ ἄρισται ἔσαν Φηρητιάδαο,
sentences.tr: hippoi men meg’ aristai esan Phērētiadao,
sentences.l: The horses, indeed, by far the best were those of Pheres’-son,
sentences.i: As for the horses, by far the best were those of the son of Pheres,
sentences.n: A new paragraph, the answer. ἵπποι μὲν is ‘the horses, for their part’, the μέν answered by ἀνδρῶν αὖ ‘of the men, in turn’ at 768. μέγ’ ἄρισται ἔσαν is ‘were by far the best’, ἄρισται being feminine because these are mares (767). Φηρητιάδαο is a patronymic in the epic genitive -αο, ‘of the son of Pheres’; the Greek does not name him here, and he is usually taken to be Admetus, the father of Eumelus, who drives them.

sentences.t:
τὰς Εὔμηλος ἔλαυνε ποδώκεας ὄρνιθας ὣς
ὄτριχας οἰέτεας σταφύλῇ ἐπὶ νῶτον ἐΐσας·
sentences.tr:
tas Eumēlos elaune podōkeas ornithas hōs
otrichas oieteas staphylēi epi nōton eïsas·
sentences.l:
which Eumelus drove, fleet-footed, like birds,
alike in hair, of one age, well-balanced along the back by the plumb-line;
sentences.i: which Eumelus drove, fleet-footed as birds, alike in hair, of one age, and well-balanced along the back as if by the plumb-line;
sentences.n: τὰς Εὔμηλος ἔλαυνε is ‘which Eumelus drove’, ἔλαυνε the unaugmented imperfect of ἐλαύνω. ποδώκεας ‘fleet-footed’ is πούς + ὠκύς, and ὄρνιθας ὣς is ‘like birds’, with ὣς set after its noun. Three words then say how well the team matches: ὄτριχας ‘alike in hair’, οἰέτεας ‘of one age’ (probably οἶος ‘one’ + ἔτος ‘year’), and ἐΐσας ‘well-balanced’, the word used of ships at 1.306, with σταφύλῃ ἐπὶ νῶτον ‘along the back by the plumb-line’, σταφύλη being a plumb-line. The exact sense of ὄτριχας and of the whole phrase is not certain.

sentences.t:
τὰς ἐν Πηρείῃ θρέψ’ ἀργυρότοξος Ἀπόλλων
ἄμφω θηλείας, φόβον Ἄρηος φορεούσας.
sentences.tr:
tas en Pēreiēi threps’ argyrotoxos Apollōn
amphō thēleias, phobon Arēos phoreousas.
sentences.l:
which in Pereia reared silver-bowed Apollo,
both female, carrying the terror of Ares.
sentences.i: which silver-bowed Apollo had reared in Pereia, both of them mares, carrying the terror of battle.
sentences.n: θρέψ’ is the elided θρέψε, an unaugmented aorist of τρέφω ‘rear’, and ἐν Πηρείῃ is ‘in Pereia’, a place of which the Greek says no more. ἀργυρότοξος Ἀπόλλων ‘silver-bowed Apollo’ is the god’s stock epithet. ἄμφω θηλείας is ‘both female’, so the pair are mares. φόβον Ἄρηος φορεούσας is ‘carrying the terror of Ares’: φόβος is ‘terror, panic’, Ἄρηος ‘of Ares’ stands for war (as at 401), and φορεούσας is the epic participle of φορέω ‘carry’.

sentences.t:
ἀνδρῶν αὖ μέγ’ ἄριστος ἔην Τελαμώνιος Αἴας
ὄφρ’ Ἀχιλεὺς μήνιεν·
sentences.tr:
andrōn au meg’ aristos eēn Telamōnios Aias
ophr’ Achileus mēnien·
sentences.l:
Of men, in turn, by far the best was Telamonian Ajax,
as long as Achilles was wrathful;
sentences.i: Of the men, in turn, by far the best was Telamonian Ajax, as long as Achilles was wrathful;
sentences.n: ἀνδρῶν αὖ ‘of the men, in turn’ answers ἵπποι μέν at 763. μέγ’ ἄριστος ἔην is ‘was by far the best’, and Τελαμώνιος Αἴας ‘Telamonian Ajax’ is told apart from the other Ajax (527) by his epithet. ὄφρ’ Ἀχιλεὺς μήνιεν is ‘as long as Achilles was wrathful’: ὄφρα is ‘as long as’, and μήνιεν is the unaugmented imperfect of μηνίω ‘be wrathful’, the verb of μῆνις; Ἀχιλεύς has a single λ for the metre. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 769.

sentences.t:
ὃ γὰρ πολὺ φέρτατος ἦεν,
ἵπποι θ’ οἳ φορέεσκον ἀμύμονα Πηλεΐωνα.
sentences.tr:
ho gar poly phertatos ēen,
hippoi th’ hoi phoreeskon amymona Pēleïōna.
sentences.l:
for he was by far the best,
and the horses that kept carrying the blameless son of Peleus.
sentences.i: for he was by far the best, and so were the horses that carried the blameless son of Peleus.
sentences.n: ὃ γάρ is ‘for he’, Achilles, and πολὺ φέρτατος ἦεν is ‘was by far the best’, φέρτατος being the superlative of φέρτερος ‘stronger’ and ἦεν the epic ἦν. The second line has no verb: ἵπποι θ’ οἳ φορέεσκον … is ‘and the horses that carried…’, sharing ‘was the best’ with Achilles. φορέεσκον is the iterative imperfect of φορέω ‘carry’, the suffix -εσκ- giving ‘kept carrying’, and ἀμύμονα Πηλεΐωνα is ‘the blameless son of Peleus’, the phrase of 674.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὃ μὲν ἐν νήεσσι κορωνίσι ποντοπόροισι
κεῖτ’ ἀπομηνίσας Ἀγαμέμνονι ποιμένι λαῶν
Ἀτρεΐδῃ·
sentences.tr:
all’ ho men en nēessi korōnisi pontoporoisi
keit’ apomēnisas Agamemnoni poimeni laōn
Atreïdēi·
sentences.i: But he lay among the curved, sea-crossing ships, withdrawn in wrath at Agamemnon, shepherd of the people, the son of Atreus;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὃ μέν is ‘but he’, Achilles. ἐν νήεσσι κορωνίσι ποντοπόροισι is ‘among the curved, sea-crossing ships’: κορωνίς ‘curved’ and ποντοπόρος ‘crossing the open sea’ are both epithets of ships in the Odyssey. κεῖτ’ is κεῖτο ‘lay’, as at 688. ἀπομηνίσας is the aorist participle of ἀπομηνίω, a rare verb built on μηνίω ‘be wrathful’ with ἀπο-. The force of ἀπο- is not certain (‘away’, ‘utterly’ and ‘ceasing’ are all proposed), and the English takes ‘having withdrawn in wrath’, with the dative Ἀγαμέμνονι ‘at Agamemnon’. ποιμένι λαῶν is ‘shepherd of the people’, and Ἀτρεΐδῃ ‘son of Atreus’ comes in the next line. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 773.

sentences.t:
λαοὶ δὲ παρὰ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης
δίσκοισιν τέρποντο καὶ αἰγανέῃσιν ἱέντες
τόξοισίν θ’·
sentences.tr:
laoi de para rhēgmini thalassēs
diskoisin terponto kai aiganeēisin hientes
toxoisin th’·
sentences.i: but the troops beside the shore where the sea breaks were amusing themselves throwing the discus and the javelin, and shooting with bows;
sentences.n: λαοὶ δὲ is ‘but the troops’, and παρὰ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης is ‘beside the surf-line of the sea’, ῥηγμίν being where the sea breaks. The second line, δίσκοισιν τέρποντο καὶ αἰγανέῃσιν ἱέντες ‘took delight with discuses and, throwing, with javelins’, is a line the Odyssey has of the suitors (4.626). τέρποντο is the imperfect middle of τέρπω ‘delight’, ἱέντες is the participle of ἵημι ‘throw, shoot’, and it governs the bows of the next half-line too: τόξοισίν θ’ is ‘and with bows’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 775.

sentences.t:
ἵπποι δὲ παρ’ ἅρμασιν οἷσιν ἕκαστος
λωτὸν ἐρεπτόμενοι ἐλεόθρεπτόν τε σέλινον
ἕστασαν·
sentences.tr:
hippoi de par’ harmasin hoisin hekastos
lōton ereptomenoi eleothrepton te selinon
hestasan·
sentences.i: and the horses stood each beside its own chariot, feeding on lotus and marsh-nurtured celery;
sentences.n: οἷσιν is the epic dative plural of the possessive ὅς, ‘their own’, and ἕκαστος ‘each one’ is singular, ‘each horse’. λωτὸν ἐρεπτόμενοι is ‘feeding on lotus’, the same two words as in the Odyssey’s land of the Lotus-eaters, where the lotus is a fruit; here λωτός is a fodder plant (the Odyssey reads it as clover in a pasture list, 4.603), and which plant either is, is not known. ἐρεπτόμενοι is the participle of ἐρέπτομαι ‘feed on’. ἐλεόθρεπτον … σέλινον is ‘marsh-nurtured celery’, from ἕλος ‘marsh’ and τρέφω ‘nurture’; σέλινον is celery or a plant like it. ἕστασαν is the pluperfect of ἵστημι, ‘stood’, with a past sense. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 777.

sentences.t:
ἅρματα δ’ εὖ πεπυκασμένα κεῖτο ἀνάκτων
ἐν κλισίῃς·
sentences.tr:
harmata d’ eu pepykasmena keito anaktōn
en klisiēis·
sentences.l:
and the chariots, well covered, lay of the lords
in the huts;
sentences.i: and the chariots of the lords lay well covered in the huts;
sentences.n: ἅρματα δ’ is ‘and the chariots’, a neuter plural, and so the verb κεῖτο ‘lay’ is singular, as Greek has it. εὖ πεπυκασμένα is ‘well covered’, the perfect passive participle of πυκάζω ‘cover closely’; ἀνάκτων ‘of the lords’ says whose they are, and ἐν κλισίῃς is ‘in the huts’, κλισίῃς being the epic dative plural of κλισίη. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 778.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἀρχὸν ἀρηΐφιλον ποθέοντες
φοίτων ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα κατὰ στρατὸν οὐδὲ μάχοντο.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ archon arēïphilon potheontes
phoitōn entha kai entha kata straton oude machonto.
sentences.l:
while they, longing for their Ares-loved commander,
went to and fro, here and there, throughout the army, and did not fight.
sentences.i: while they, missing their commander, dear to Ares, went to and fro, this way and that, through the army, and did not fight.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘but they’ are the men, as against the horses and the chariots. ἀρχὸν ἀρηΐφιλον ποθέοντες is ‘longing for their Ares-loved commander’: ἀρηΐφιλος ‘dear to Ares’ is the Odyssey’s epithet of Menelaus, and ποθέοντες is the participle of ποθέω as at 703; the commander is Achilles, who is not named. φοίτων is the imperfect of φοιτάω ‘go to and fro’, ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα is ‘here and there’, κατὰ στρατόν is ‘through the army’, and οὐδὲ μάχοντο is ‘and did not fight’, μάχοντο being the epic imperfect. With this the Catalogue ends on the army idle by the sea.
